analysis.investment_thesis: At a P/E of 20 and ROE of a paltry 0.21%, Indobell Insulation offers no margin of safety and fails nearly every quantitative screen I require. This is a recently-listed micro-cap (INR 44.9 Cr) with negligible earning power — precisely the speculative territory I counsel investors to avoid.
key_strengths: Long operating history since 1972 provides business continuity
High promoter holding at 65% signals insider commitment
Operates in a tangible, understandable industrial product category
key_risks: ROE of 0.21% indicates essentially no productive use of shareholder capital
P/E of 20 exceeds my 15 ceiling — price detached from earning power
Micro-cap (INR 44.9 Cr) with no visible dividend history or balance-sheet disclosure
red_flags: ROE near zero — the business is barely earning on its equity base
Recently listed IPO-type security lacking the 5-year earnings record I demand
No data on current ratio, debt/equity, or book value — cannot verify solvency
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The numbers condemn this security from my perspective. A 0.21% ROE means the business is earning virtually nothing on its capital — a fixed deposit would do dramatically better with zero risk. Yet Mr. Market is asking 20 times earnings, which implies an earnings yield of 5% against a near-zero return on equity. That is the definition of speculation on future improvement, not investment in demonstrated earning power. I cannot compute a Graham Number without book value per share, but the combination of 20x P/E and 0.21% ROE makes any reasonable intrinsic value calculation produce a figure far below market price.

Equally troubling is the absence of the data a defensive investor requires: no current ratio, no debt-to-equity, no interest coverage, no dividend record. A 54-year-old company that only recently came to the public markets with a market cap of INR 44.9 Cr fits the classic profile of a small promoter-driven issue where the seller knows far more than the buyer. The 65% promoter stake is the only mild positive, but insider ownership does not rescue miserable economics. I would require a price closer to 30–40% of book value and demonstrated earnings stability before considering this — conditions not remotely met here.
